Days of therapy fell by 11 percent at introduction, with no further trend, and the fall was largest for carbapenems and anti-pseudomonal penicillins. Acceptance of recommendations was 74 percent. Rates of C. difficile infection, 30-day mortality and readmission did not change. Two hospitals changed their empirical guidelines during the study, which may account for part of the fall."},{"title":"Handshake stewardship versus remote written review on surgical wards: acceptance of recommendations and antimicrobial use","authors":"Bellamy-Chukwu T, Sorensen-Iqbal M","year":2023,"venue":"Surgical Infection Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"On six surgical wards of two hospitals, we compared quarters of in-person handshake rounds with quarters of remote written review over 18 months, alternating by quarter. Acceptance was 81 percent with handshake rounds and 52 percent with written review. Days of therapy were 9 percent lower in handshake quarters. Handshake rounds took about 3 more pharmacist hours per ward per week. Surgeons valued discussing the duration of prophylaxis in person. The alternating design reduced but did not remove the influence of secular trends."},{"title":"Why surgeons decline stewardship recommendations: a thematic analysis of 38 conversations","authors":"Okoro-Lindberg A, Fairclough-Tan W","year":2021,"venue":"Infection and Hospital Teams","doi":"10.5555/iht.2021.0402","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed 38 conversations with surgeons and surgical trainees about antimicrobial stewardship recommendations they had declined. Themes included uncertainty about who was responsible for antimicrobial decisions on the team, recommendations arriving after the ward round when plans were fixed, a sense that written notes from pharmacists lacked clinical context, and fear of infection in patients with implants. Recommendations discussed in person and early in the day were described as easier to act on. Participants suggested that the most senior surgeon present should be the named recipient."},{"title":"Prescriber experience of audit and feedback in intensive care: hierarchy, timing and trust","authors":"Rautenbach-Oyelaran S, Moreau-Khalil J","year":2018,"venue":"Critical Care Team Studies","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held focus groups with 26 intensivists, trainees and critical care pharmacists in three intensive care units about stewardship feedback. Participants described feedback as welcome when delivered at the daily multidisciplinary round by a pharmacist who was part of the unit team, and as intrusive when it came from outside. Trainees reported that they could not act on recommendations without consultant agreement. Trust built over months of joint rounds, and turnover of pharmacists reset it. Nurses were often the ones who reminded the team of stop dates."},{"title":"Mapping outcome measures in antimicrobial stewardship evaluations: a review of 142 studies","authors":"Thibodeaux-Ansah P, Hollingsworth-Emeka D, Varga-Sato C","year":2022,"venue":"Stewardship Methods Review","doi":"10.5555/smr.2022.0356","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We catalogued the outcome measures used in 142 evaluations of hospital stewardship interventions. Days of therapy were reported in 61 percent, defined daily doses in 38 percent and both in 12 percent. Clinical outcomes were reported by 44 percent, most often mortality, and C. difficile by 33 percent. Only 19 percent reported acceptance of recommendations, and 7 percent reported pharmacist time. Denominators differed between patient-days, admissions and days present, which prevents direct comparison. The authors propose days of therapy per 1000 days present as a common measure."},{"title":"Clostridioides difficile infection and mortality after stewardship audit and feedback programmes: a pooled analysis of 17 hospitals","authors":"Gallagher-Nwosu E, Pietersen-Liu H","year":2016,"venue":"Hospital Epidemiology Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We pooled data from 17 hospitals that introduced audit and feedback between 2008 and 2013 and compared the incidence of hospital-onset C. difficile infection and in-hospital mortality in the two years before and after. C. difficile incidence fell by 18 percent, but the fall was concentrated in hospitals that also restricted fluoroquinolones at the same time. In-hospital mortality did not change. Hospitals with fewer than 200 beds contributed 4 of the 17 sites and showed wider variation. The authors caution that concurrent restriction policies make attribution difficult."},{"title":"Pharmacist workload and recommendation acceptance in stewardship audit and feedback: a time-and-motion study","authors":"Kaminski-Adjei L, Brandvold-Osei R","year":2024,"venue":"Journal of Antimicrobial Stewardship Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We timed stewardship pharmacists' audit and feedback work over 40 weekdays at three hospitals. Reviewing a patient took a median of 7 minutes, writing a recommendation 4 minutes, and an in-person discussion 6 minutes. Pharmacists covering more than 30 patients a day wrote shorter recommendations, and acceptance fell from 76 to 61 percent as daily caseload rose. Community hospital sites had the longest travel and waiting times for in-person discussion. The authors estimate that extending audit and feedback to surgical wards would need about 0.5 additional pharmacist FTE per 100 beds."},{"title":"Nurses' role in stewardship feedback rounds: perspectives from ward teams","authors":"Achterberg-Duarte M, Nkemelu-Frost J","year":2019,"venue":"Nursing Stewardship Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/nsq.2019.0088","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held 22 conversations with ward nurses, nurse managers and stewardship pharmacists on medical and surgical wards about how stewardship recommendations are passed on. Nurses described themselves as the link between the pharmacist's note and the team, reminding doctors of review dates and intravenous-to-oral switches. They felt their role was invisible in stewardship reports and that recommendations written only in the chart were often missed. Several suggested that nurses attend handshake rounds when possible. The findings come from two hospitals with established stewardship teams."},{"title":"Sustaining audit and feedback after programme funding ends: a five-year follow-up of three hospitals","authors":"Lemaire-Boateng C, Yilmaz-Carrow T","year":2025,"venue":"Stewardship Methods Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed three hospitals for five years after dedicated funding for audit and feedback ended. Two hospitals kept the service with existing pharmacists but reviewed fewer patients a day, and days of therapy drifted back up by 6 percent over three years. The third hospital stopped audit and feedback and returned to its pre-programme level within 18 months. Sites that kept in-person rounds maintained higher acceptance. The authors suggest planning staffing for the long term before extending programmes to new wards or sites."}]}
